title: Thailand: Two Uyghurs at Risk of Return to China
content:
(Bangkok) – Thai authorities should not forcibly return two Uyghur men to China, where they face grave risks of torture and other serious abuses, Human Rights Watch said today. The two men, whose names are not public for security reasons, were transferred from prison to immigration detention in Bangkok after receiving a royal pardon, apparently in preparation for deportation.

“Previous Thai governments have kept Uyghurs in inhumane detention for years and then complied with Beijing’s demands to send them to China, where they were forcibly disappeared,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul should end forced returns to China and allow the two Uyghur men to travel to a safe third country.”

title: Japan: Raise Rights With Vietnam’s Leader
content:
(Tokyo) – Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi should urge Vietnamese President To Lam to make concrete progress on human rights during his official visit to Japan from November 8 to 11, 2026, Human Rights Watch said today.

Human Rights Watch wrote to Prime Minister Takaichi expressing concerns about Vietnam’s intensifying crackdown on human rights. The repression violates obligations that Vietnam accepted under the 2018 Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership, to which Vietnam and Japan are parties.

“The Vietnamese government has broken its pledges for reform and continues to crack down on basic freedoms,” said Kanae Doi, Japan director at Human Rights Watch. “Prime Minister Takaichi should communicate clearly and publicly to President To Lam Japan’s serious concerns about human rights and labor rights violations.”

The Vietnamese government has sharply intensified its repression of basic freedoms over the past decade, Human Rights Watch said. To Lam served as Vietnam’s minister of public security from 2016 to 2024, heading the country’s national police force. He is now both general secretary of the Communist Party of Vietnam and president.

title: Changes to Chile’s Human Rights Institute Risk Leaving Victims Behind
content:
Chilean President José Antonio Kast introduced in Congress on October 19 a proposal to change the country’s National Human Rights Institute.

Founded in 2009 as an autonomous state body, the institute has worked to promote and protect human rights in Chile, including by taking legal action on behalf of human rights abuse victims.

If passed, the legislation would weaken some of the tools the institute uses to protect human rights and diminish its independence.

The bill would remove the institute’s eleven-member board of directors, replacing them with a new five-member transitional board that would draft new bylaws for the institute. Unlike the current board, which has four members who were selected directly by civil society groups, the new transitional board would be proposed by the president, approved by the Senate, and would have no members selected directly by civil society. This sits uneasily with the standards set out in the Principles relating to the Status of National Human Rights Institutions (the Paris Principles), which recommend that members be independent from the government and selected through a process that ensures broad civil society representation.

title: Ethiopian Authorities Suspend Independent Newspaper
content:
In what has become the new normal, the Ethiopian government has silenced yet another independent media outlet.

The Ethiopian Media Authority announced in a November 2 Facebook post that it is indefinitely suspending the print and online license of the Reporter, one of Ethiopia’s oldest media institutions. Publishing in English and Amharic, the Reporter is also the country’s last privately owned Amharic newspaper.

Stating that the suspension would take effect immediately, the Media Authority accused the Reporter of violating the country’s laws and media ethics by repeatedly publishing content that was against “national interests.” The authority added that the outlet published “distorted content that negatively affects foreign investment, tourism, and diplomacy.”

The action is part of the government’s ongoing assault on the media and civic space in the country and points toward increasing use of vague claims about “national interests” to shut down any critical reporting.

title: World Court Set to Rule in Myanmar Genocide Case
content:
(The Hague) – The International Court of Justice has announced that it will deliver its judgment on November 19, 2026, in the case brought by Gambia against Myanmar for alleged violations of the Genocide Convention, Human Rights Watch said today in releasing a question-and-answer document on key issues in the case.

In August 2017, Myanmar’s security forces began a sweeping campaign of massacres, rape, and arson against ethnic Rohingya in northern Rakhine State that forced more than 700,000 people to flee to neighboring Bangladesh. In November 2019, Gambia filed a case before the International Court of Justice alleging that Myanmar’s atrocities against the Rohingya constitute genocide and violate the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide. This is not a criminal case against individuals, but a request for a legal determination of Myanmar’s state responsibility for genocide.

title: Türkiye: European Court to Rule on Istanbul Mayor’s Detention
content:
The Turkish authorities are misusing powers of detention and prosecution against opposition politicians in Türkiye to prevent them from participating effectively in elections or political life, the Turkey Litigation Support Project, Human Rights Watch, and the International Commission of Jurists said today.

The three groups have submitted a third-party intervention—or amicus brief—to the European Court of Human Rights with information on patterns of human rights violations, abuse of the criminal law, and the erosion of judicial independence in Türkiye. The intervention was made in a case brought by the Istanbul mayor and opposition politician Ekrem İmamoğlu to the Strasbourg court asserting that his detention violates his rights protected under provisions of the European Convention on Human Rights, including article 5 (right to liberty and security), article 18 (limitation on use of restrictions on rights), and article 3 of Protocol No. 1 to the convention (right to free elections).

title: Zambia: Widespread Repression in Post-Election Crackdown
content:
(Johannesburg) – The Zambian police and military forcibly disappeared, arbitrarily detained, beat, and threatened opposition members and supporters as well as lawyers, journalists, and government critics in the days before and after general elections in August 2026, Human Rights Watch said today. The authorities have also yet to credibly explain or investigate the killing of an opposition leader in contested circumstances.

“Zambia’s government should break this dangerous cycle of repression,” said Ashwanee Budoo-Scholtz, deputy Africa director at Human Rights Watch. “The authorities should immediately halt the ongoing post-election crackdown, allow access to lawyers and provide medical care for those in detention, release everyone arbitrarily detained, and ensure accountability for abuses by security forces.”

title: Australia: Solitary Confinement Harming Prisoners with Disabilities
content:
(Sydney) — Prison authorities in the Australian state of South Australia are harming people with disabilities by using solitary confinement, Human Rights Watch said in a report released today.

The 50-page report, “‘They Just Locked Me Away’: Solitary Confinement and Abuse of People with Disabilities in Prisons in the State of South Australia,” documents the use of solitary confinement on people with psychosocial disabilities, mental health conditions. It details broader problems facing people with disabilities in South Australian prisons, including inadequate access to individualized mental health care and lack of prison oversight.

title: Pakistan: Rights Lawyers Receive 10-Year Sentences
content:
(New York) – An anti-terrorism court in Pakistan imposed 10-year prison sentences on two human rights lawyers on October 29, 2026, in an escalation of the government’s crackdown on civil society, Human Rights Watch said today. Pakistani authorities should immediately quash the convictions, release Imaan Mazari-Hazir and her husband Hadi Ali Chattha, and cease criminal proceedings aimed at punishing human rights advocates.

The sentences were handed down following a trial held inside Adiala prison in Rawalpindi. The lawyers were accused of obstructing police at a road closure in Islamabad in October 2024. 

Instead of prosecuting them for a misdemeanor or common crime, the police charged them under Pakistan’s anti-terrorism act, which carries far greater penalties and a longer sentence. This was the second time in recent weeks that the two have been prosecuted in an apparent attempt to prevent them from carrying out their legal work.

title: New US Sanctions Target Rwanda’s Abusive Role in Eastern Congo
content: The United States Treasury announced new sanctions this week against Rwanda's Ministry of Defense and Zigama Credit and Savings Society, a Rwandan financial institution that the US Treasury found facilitated payments for the Rwandan army and the abusive M23 armed group. The sanctions freeze all named parties’ assets and interests in the US and effectively bar their use of the US dollar in international transactions.

title: “They Killed Us”
content:
When I woke up this morning to the news that Novaya Gazeta is closing its doors, it felt like a personal blow. To me, Novaya’s office in a small grey building in central Moscow always felt like home. 

The newsroom moved to Moscow almost three decades ago. I got to know its every nook and cranny, as I went there, in my capacity of a Moscow-based Human Rights Watch researcher, for meetings, celebrations, commemorations, or simply to swap stories with a friendly journalist over coffee or wine.

I was there on the night of Anna Politkovskaya’s murder in October 2006 and stood outside seven years later as her memorial plaque was affixed to the wall. I celebrated with the newsroom when editor-in-chief Dmitry Muratov won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2021. For years, I worked alongside Novaya journalists in conflict zones. Together, we travelled to Chechnya, remote mountain villages in Dagestan, South Ossetia (Georgia), and Ukraine. It was more than collaboration; it was a true partnership.

title: Critic of Mali’s Junta Forcibly Disappeared Six Months On
content:
Six months after their abductions, Mountaga Tall, an outspoken critic of Mali’s junta, and his son, Cheick Mamadou Tall, remain missing, their fate unknown, and the Malian authorities silent. Every day that passes without news raises fears for their safety and deepens their family’s anguish.

Unidentified gunmen abducted Tall in Bamako, Mali’s capital, on May 2. Tall’s son went missing on May 16 after receiving a call informing him that he could deliver belongings to his father, who was reportedly being held at an undisclosed location.

Radio France Internationale reported in July that the United Nations Committee on Enforced Disappearances had urged Mali’s authorities to locate and protect Tall and his son.

International media suggest that Malian intelligence services may be holding Tall in a secret facility. Malian authorities, however, have neither acknowledged detaining Tall or his son nor provided information about their location, legal status, or health, despite requests from Tall’s family and a legal team.

title: Women Should Never Give Birth in Shackles
content:
An incarcerated Indigenous woman was reportedly shackled during a hospital stay earlier this month to deliver her baby by caesarean section in a Queensland hospital in Australia.

Queensland Corrective Services promised an internal review but did not confirm the shackling. Shackling a woman during childbirth contravenes international human rights standards.

The incident happened days before Australia’s two major political parties blocked a vote in parliament on October 14 on a bill to ban the shackling of prisoners during childbirth. United Nations human rights experts criticized the Australian parliament’s failure to vote on the bill.

Prisoners and detainees do not lose their rights to health or to be treated humanely and with dignity. Restraining a woman during childbirth raises grave concerns about degrading treatment and interference with care, which constitute obstetric violence.

Obstetric violence is the physical and emotional abuse of pregnant people seeking sexual and reproductive health services and information, including maternal health. It is a form of gender-based violence and a violation of fundamental human rights.

title: Mbappé, Mao, and La Liga
content:
This week a Chinese sports forum unearthed an April 2026 interview with Real Madrid football star Kylian Mbappé jokingly likening himself to a “Chinese dictator” (dictateur chinois). While Mbappé, known for dictating terms on the pitch, did not name names, the broadcaster added art showing him as Chinese Communist Party founder Mao Zedong.

Beijing’s reaction was swift. China’s Foreign Ministry claimed the words “hurt the feelings of the Chinese people.” Chinese state broadcaster CCTV blacked out all Spanish football league La Liga matches.

The Chinese Communist Party under Xi Jinping has low tolerance for anything that could be interpreted as an affront to China, even a comment about Mao made in jest. Javier Tebas, the Spanish football league’s president, issued an apology praising La Liga’s ties with China’s “government departments.”

title: UN Finds Age-Based Persecution of Palestinian Children
content:
A UN Commission of Inquiry concluded on October 14 that Israeli authorities have committed the crime against humanity of persecution against Palestinian children. Their findings recognize an important dimension that has not been given enough attention: children in the West Bank have been deliberately targeted—not just because of their nationality, race or ethnicity but also due to their age—in attacks causing serious bodily and mental harm. 

After making the same determination about Gaza in June, the commission expanded its finding to the West Bank, explaining: “the harm inflicted on children is not incidental or collateral to the broader violence affecting civilian population, but forms part of a pattern of intentional violence.” 

Age-based persecution is not limited to Gaza or the West Bank. Last November, judges at the International Criminal Court confirmed 39 charges, albeit in absentia, against Joseph Kony, leader of the Lord’s Resistance Army, for crimes in northern Uganda including persecution on age grounds.

title: Activist in DR Congo Faces Military Trial
content:
More than three months have passed since plainclothes security officers arrested pro-democracy activist Clovis Kakule Mutsuva on July 18 in North Kivu province in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. Mutsuva, 32, is awaiting trial before a military court on several charges.

The Allied Democratic Forces, a Ugandan-origin armed group active in eastern Congo, has been carrying out deadly attacks in the North Kivu city of Beni, near the Ugandan border. Mutsuva and other activists used videos and public speeches to call for a city-wide shutdown of public activities.

The shutdown, which was peaceful according to Beni’s mayor, occurred on May 14.Nonetheless, two months later Mutsuva was arrested and charged with incitement to disobey the law, criticizing public authority, organizing unauthorized demonstrations, insulting the army, spreading false rumors, and spreading false information on social media. The prosecution has accused Mutsuva of calling on demonstrators to “set fire” to the streets at night in protest of insecurity and to demand that the government protect civilians.

title: US: New Hurdles to Having Votes Counted
content:
(Washington, DC) – US states’ use of a tool to verify citizenship that is marred by inaccurate and incomplete data is creating new hurdles for the right to vote with the midterm elections only days away, Human Rights Watch said today. The Supreme Court ruled in late September 2026 that states could use the tool, Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE), to screen lists of registered voters for citizenship status, at least for the time being.

“The use of the SAVE tool is causing new hurdles for some voters,” said Katherine La Puente, US democracy researcher at Human Rights Watch. “Sending vaguely worded letters as early voting began or offering federal-only ballots to some registered voters risks a discriminatory impact on people’s right to vote.”

title: Sri Lanka: Organized Crime Bill Violates Rights Standards
content:
(New York) – The Sri Lankan government’s Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill, submitted to parliament on October 20, 2026, risks enabling arbitrary detention, torture, and other rights violations, Human Rights Watch said today. The proposed law, alongside the Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill submitted on October 6, reproduces abusive provisions in existing counterterrorism laws that would allow continuing abuses that the government had pledged to end.

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake’s National People’s Power alliance pledged in its 2024 election manifesto to abolish all “oppressive” laws and ensure “civil rights of people in all parts of the country.” In particular, the Dissanayake government—like its predecessors—pledged to repeal the notorious Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA). Both bills presented in October replicate some of the worst aspects of the PTA, shifting abusive provisions to create parallel legal structures outside existing criminal law and without basic safeguards.

title: Yemen: Houthis Depriving Taizz Civilians of Food, Medicine
content:
(Beirut) – A long-running humanitarian crisis in Taizz, Yemen’s third-largest city, has drastically worsened since October 2026, when the Houthi armed group forces fully encircled the city and blocked and attacked the remaining major supply route, Human Rights Watch said today. Since then, there have been severe shortages of fuel, food, water, medicine, cooking gas, and access by humanitarian agencies.

Houthi forces have surrounded Taizz since 2015, early in the conflict with the Yemeni government. While government-backed forces control the city center, Houthi forces have blocked access to all major roads connecting Taizz to the rest of the country, with the road connecting Taizz with Aden the most important. While international law does not prohibit sieges of military forces, the Houthis’ siege has for 11 years severely restricted civilian movement and impeded essential goods to the city’s residents.

title: India: Mass Voter Roll Exclusions Deeply Flawed
content:
(London) – The Indian authorities’ removal of over 130 million names from the country’s electoral rolls is arbitrary and deeply flawed, Human Rights Watch said today.

In October 2026, tens of thousands of people across India began demonstrating against the Election Commission of India’s Special Intensive Revision (SIR). The process purportedly removed dead, duplicate, or ineligible voters, but has been arbitrary and opaque and has disproportionately excluded women, people living in poverty, religious minorities, especially Muslims, and people from other marginalized communities. In October, the Election Commission submitted an affidavit to the Supreme Court defending its functioning and rejecting all allegations of irregularities.

“Indian authorities first stripped millions of citizens of their right to vote and are now beating and jailing them for peacefully protesting these rights violations,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “The authorities should immediately scrap the voter roll revision process that has denied India’s most marginalized people their right to vote and other government services.”
snippet: (London) – The Indian authorities’ removal of over 130 million names from the country’s electoral rolls is arbitrary and deeply flawed, Human Rights Watch said today.
